big_idea: Positional words describe LOCATION. Above, below, beside, inside, outside, between.
learning_intention: We are learning to describe location with positional words.
student_learning_goal: I can describe location with positional words.
success_criteria: I can describe where an object is.
I can place an object using a position word.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Sammy and Mira — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Lesson 3 positional tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Mira made a map. The lion is ABOVE the river. The zebra is BELOW the tree. Where is the elephant?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Sammy + Mira puppets. 'Yesterday we named shapes. Today Mira helps us describe LOCATION using POSITION words.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write ABOVE, BELOW, BESIDE on chart. Add INSIDE, OUTSIDE, BETWEEN.

Demonstrate with safari map. 'The lion is ABOVE the river — on top, higher.' Place lion above. 'The zebra is BELOW the tree — under, lower.' Place zebra below. 'The elephant is BESIDE the lion — next to.' Place elephant beside.

More demos: 'INSIDE the cave — within. OUTSIDE the cage — not within. BETWEEN two trees — in the middle.'

Real-life examples: 'Your bag is BESIDE your chair. The clock is ABOVE the door. Your shoes are BELOW your desk.'

'Mira says — position words tell us EXACTLY where. We use them to describe and find things.'

Sammy's RULE: 'NAME IT — count SIDES — count CORNERS!' Today we adapt: NAME the position — POINT to the THING — say WHERE.

Class refrain. Class chants 3x with claps: 'NAME IT — count SIDES — count CORNERS! That's how Sammy hunts!'

'Today we use position words to describe and place objects.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: practice 6 position words with classroom objects.
Three stations. Station A: Place safari animals on map using position cards. Station B: Describe positions in pictures. Station C: Pair-and-place: one says, partner places.
Stretch challenge at Station C: use 2 position words ('above and beside').
Discuss meaning. 'Above = higher. Below = lower. Beside = next to. Inside = within. Outside = not within. Between = in middle.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Show position chart with arrow examples.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the positional tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Mark the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Above/below/beside only — skip inside/outside/between.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station C: 2-word combinations ('above and beside the river').
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Sentence frame: 'The ___ is ___ the ___.' Pre-teach each position word with a clear hand gesture (above = palm overhead; below = palm lowered; beside = hand to side; inside = hand cupped; outside = hand pointing away; between = hands forming a sandwich).
differentiation.for_movement_learners: NO-PAPER, NO-PURCHASE PATH: skip the printed map and animal tokens. Children become the safari — they physically place themselves ABOVE (standing on a chair), BELOW (sitting on the floor), BESIDE (next to a partner), INSIDE (in a hula-hoop or marked square), OUTSIDE (outside the marked area), BETWEEN (between two classmates). Teacher calls a position word; children move there. Whole lesson runs on bodies + classroom space — no purchased map, no animal tokens, no position cards.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: uses 5+ position words; describes locations; places objects.

discussion_prompts: What's the difference between INSIDE and OUTSIDE?
Where is your bag right now?
consolidation.exit_routine: Refrain chant 3x. Then each child describes ONE classroom item using a precise position word: 'The ___ is ___ the ___.' Sticky-note one position description and post on the Shape Safari poster.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child uses 'over' or 'on' for everything — repairing the position-word generalisation at K (Clements & Sarama, 2009; Levine et al., 2012; Pruden, Levine & Huttenlocher, 2011)
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On A9.3 positional language, the most-documented K trap is the over-everything generalisation: child says 'the cat is OVER the mat' for almost every position. They have not yet differentiated the position-word lattice (above, below, beside, inside, outside, between) into precise spatial categories.

Clements & Sarama (2009) place positional vocabulary as a foundational K skill in their spatial reasoning trajectory — children who exit K with only 1-2 position words are limited in geometric reasoning, mapping, and mental rotation tasks for several grades after.

Levine, Ratliff, Huttenlocher & Cannon (2012) showed empirically that K children's spatial language exposure (the number and variety of position words they hear and use at home and school) correlates with later spatial reasoning outcomes — including STEM-relevant skills like graph reading and 3D visualisation. The intervention they tested was simple: K teachers DELIBERATELY model 6+ position words across the school day, and prompt children to use them in talk. This lesson is engineered to do exactly that.

Pruden, Levine & Huttenlocher (2011) traced individual differences in K spatial language and found that children at risk of spatial-reasoning gaps benefit MOST from explicit position-word instruction with embodied placement — children placing their bodies in spatial positions, not just hearing words.

Why this matters: a K child who uses one position word for everything ('over' or 'there') is behind on the spatial-language trajectory in a way that compounds through Grade 3. The repair is simple but must be explicit: insist on precise vocabulary, with embodied placement.

The walkthrough covers when child overuses 'over'.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station A. Child places lion 'over' the river. Says 'over' for elephant beside lion too.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'Lion is OVER, yes — but elephant is BESIDE, not over. Beside means NEXT TO, same level.'

Walk through. 'Above = HIGHER. Below = LOWER. Beside = SAME LEVEL.'

The child re-describes. Generalise. 'Mira says — pick the RIGHT position word. Each one means something different.'

If still using 'over' for everything: provide position-word cards. 'Pick from these.' Force diverse use.

Long-term recovery: every position description checks the precise word.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Uses one word for all positions.
common_misconceptions: Over = anywhere. (Repair: position words are precise.)
All higher = above. (Repair: above means directly higher.)
Beside means in front. (Repair: beside means at same level, next to.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child uses one word ('over') for every position: provide a position-word fan card with all 6 words. Child must point at the matching card BEFORE saying the position. Force the differentiation. Repeat for the next 4 placements until child reaches for different cards spontaneously.

DIAGNOSTIC B — child knows above/below/beside but mixes inside/outside/between: physically demonstrate with a hula-hoop or marked square. Child stands INSIDE the hoop while saying 'inside'; steps OUT while saying 'outside'; stands BETWEEN two hoops. Embodied placement (Pruden, Levine & Huttenlocher 2011) for the harder words.

DIAGNOSTIC C — child uses position words but reverses them (says 'above' for below, etc.): pair adjacent placements ('place lion ABOVE the rock — now place lion BELOW the rock'); contrast forces the differentiation. If the reversal persists, anchor to gesture: above = palm overhead; below = palm at feet. Tick 'uses 5+ position words' only after 3 unprompted correct uses in a row.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of A9.3 and A9.6.

parts_outline.task: Look at 4 pictures. Write the position word.
Place 4 animals on the map by position.

expected_image_assets: Map with 4 placement spots for Part 2
